utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we -- when we left off yesterday, we were still talking about 12 July, events of that day and what you saw and experienced in Potocari. One thing you talked about, you told us yesterday about the conversation with Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic before you went to Potocari about what would happen to the men and to the women and children, and you told us about what you saw when you were there in Potocari, the mistreatment and that you realised that things were not going the way they should have, and you talked that there were some men placed on the first convoy but only on the first convoy. Can you tell me about whether that first convoy was filmed and your conclusion as to why it was filmed, if it was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation, and something of what you said I understood, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, are you now hearing me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I can hear the interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll ask it again, Mr. Nikolic. Yesterday, we were talking about the 12th of July and what you saw and experienced in Potocari with the separations of the men. You told us about your conversation with Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic before you went to Potocari, the mistreatment of the men in Potocari and that you realised things were not going as the way they should be done. And you talked about how some men were put on the first convoy out. Now, I want to ask you whether that convoy -- that process of men getting onto the first bus, I should say, not first convoy, that on the first group to leave there were some men. Was that process filmed, and if it was, why did you conclude that that part of the process had been filmed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I know, in fact what I saw is that for some time in Potocari the press centre from the Drina Corps command was present. I know those people personally, and I know their chief, their head, Captain Zoran. There were other teams as well, but I'm referring to this service that is part of the Drina Corps command of my superior command. They were filming that, and all I can do is express my opinion, which I have done on numerous occasions to date. I will repeat it. In the first convoy alone there were men, and this was filmed. Given the way in which events subsequently unfolded, the only conclusion I could draw was that this was filmed for the benefit of DutchBat representatives and for the purpose of spreading propaganda by this press department, by the journalists who were part of a given command. And, in fact, in that film, in those videos, one attempted to demonstrate that everything was fine, that everything was being done in accordance with the rules, but, in fact, my impression was that all this was done for the purpose of propaganda, because only the first convoy and only one convoy was filmed and nothing else after that, apart from that process of film being certain soldiers and officers who gave statements about all the events were also filmed. Positive opinions were expressed. I would say that no one who participated in that operation was incriminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can you clarify for me. Were the men on the first bus or the first convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The men were in the first convoy. I won't claim that they were in each and every bus, but in -- in terms of percentage, 90 per cent of the buses in the first convoy there were a few men at least. I can't really provide you with any precise figures, it is impossible, but I could see in the buses of the first convoy there were men. They would enter as the buses arrived. One bus would arrive and then the family with a man would enter the bus. A brother, a father - it doesn't really matter - would enter. Then the next bus would arrive and some men would enter the next bus as well. So I am speaking about the first convoy, not the first bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How long did you spend in Potocari that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, on the 12th, as I have already said I was the duty officer on at that day, and occasionally I spent some time in Potocari, and when I wasn't in Potocari, I was in the operations room where I was the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. When you arrived in Potocari on the 12th after the last Hotel Fontana meeting, how long did you stay there before you returned to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first occasion not very long, perhaps 30 minutes, perhaps a little less. But I didn't spend a long time there. The first time I went there I didn't spend much time in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when did you come back that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went to Potocari on a number of occasions on that day, so I really cannot tell you exactly when I returned. I can't give you the exact hour or minute. I returned on a number of occasions because I would do so whenever it was necessary to return to deal with certain questions or certain problems that had arisen. I can mention a few problems that I, myself, dealt with, but the first time I went there I know that I saw Mr. Kingori, Major Kingori, who was part of the military observers team. He said that they had no water. So I went to Bratunac and water was delivered to Potocari by truck. I know that he also complained that the soldiers who entered Potocari had taken equipment and food and other things from them at a check-point in Potocari. He also complained that the soldiers who entered disarmed some UNPROFOR soldiers who weren't at their base in Potocari, who were outside their base. So that was the first time. The next time I went there was because there were problems regarding the passage of convoys. The convoy transporting Muslims from Potocari to Kladanj was targeted. They threw stones at it, in fact, and I was told that there were problems with the convoy that was passing through urban areas. So that's about a distance of 700 metres or 1 kilometre, and it was on that stretch of road that they stoned the convoy. I contacted the civilian police, I contacted the command of the military police, and we provided security for that stretch of road so that the convoy could pass through safely and so that we could prevent the buses, the wind screens from being broken and so on and so forth. So these were practical problems I had to deal with when I went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you were there when the transport began. Can you tell us about approximately what time that was in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was between 1.00 and 2.00 that the buses started arriving one by one, and as they arrived, the transport command -- or, rather, they would fill up the buses. When the buses arrived, they formed a convoy out of the buses that arrived. This was a continual process. New buses kept arriving. Some left. They formed these columns and then they would leave and others would arrive. So this is how this evacuation was done -- or, rather, this is how these people from Potocari were moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And when do you remember it ended on that day on the 12th, when the last buses with people on them left?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening hours, but I really don't know. Don't ask me to tell you but it was in the evening hours. I knew exactly when. I knew the time because I was the duty officer on the day and I made a note of such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to speculate, but it was in the evening hours of that first day. It took a long time. It was before night fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could I have 65 ter 22820, please. While this is coming up, I don't want to go over it again because you explained it, but you talked yesterday about Vujadin Popovic being in Potocari, as well as members of state security or RDB. This document is dated 12 July 1995, headed Drina Corps IKM, forward command post. It's from Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic. Very urgent. And it says: "To the Main Staff of the VRS, sector for intelligence and security affairs. Security administration. Command of the Drina Corps. Security Department." If we could scroll down so that the witness can see paragraph 3. It is on the next page in the English. There we see: "A refugee group of about 30- to 35.000 women, children, elderly, and infirm and the sick is located after beyond the UNPROFOR base towards Srebrenica, on the road and inside the facilities of the former factories. The security was established and the evacuation to Kladanj started. About 5.000 women and children were evacuated so far. We are separating men from 17 to 60 years of age and we are not transporting them. We have about 70 of them so far and the security organs and the DB are working with them." And it's got a stamp. It's hard to read. It sayings received January 12, 1934 on the bottom right. And I should have said on the top -- if we go back up to the top of the front first page in the English. We see that under the date of 12 July it says 1730 hours. You spoke about after the first convoy all the men were separated and detained. I want you to comment on whether this paragraph 3 written by Vujadin Popovic, the Drina Corps security chief, that he is reporting up to all these different organs is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see who Mr. Popovic is reporting to at the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the numbers look accurate to you that he quotes, at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a higher number -- or, rather, I don't think so. I'm sure, I'm absolutely sure because I saw this myself. Could you just scroll up so I could see the figure. Is says that about 70 of them. I am claiming that there were between 350 and 400 of them who had been separated on that day, singled out. That's what I know for sure. And at the time that the report was made, well, the hour is 1730 hours. At that time, my claim is that there were far more than 70 of them. And in the last paragraph, it says that the security organs and members of the state security sector were involved in this process of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nikolic, the last sentence you read, i.e., We have about 70 of them so far and the security organs and the state security are working with them. The security organs refer to -- refer to you. So security organs on the ground means you. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The organs on the ground -- at the time there were several security organs on the ground at the time. It's true that I was also part of the security organs, and I was also present in Potocari. That is also true. But there were other security organs there. Security organs from the Drina Corps were present, or the chief of the intelligence organ from the Drina Corps was there, and there were other security organs there, not just myself and Popovic. There were others from other units, because all units have -- this includes those from Potocari. All units have security organs as an integral part of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll give the next Prosecution exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4388, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday as well, you gave your estimate of a thousand, 1.500 or 2.000 men at the time who were in the column moving from Srebrenica towards -- to Potocari and then who gathered there, and you stated that it was your assessment that many of them -- or that they were not all soldiers. As security and intelligence chief in Bratunac at that time, all these men who were separated after the first convoy left, amongst them, were there men - the men referred to in Popovic's report - who were not soldiers, who had not committed any crimes against the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either the interpretation is not correct or there's some other problem, but I don't really understand what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask it again. I'll make it simpler. Among all the men who were separated in Potocari who we have been talking about, were there men who were just plain civilians, who were not soldiers and had not committed any crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment, and this is what I have always claimed and I still make this claim, most of the people, the men who were separated in Potocari, this is on the basis of what I know, most of them shouldn't have been separated for any reason or any military reason. To single someone out, to separate someone, you have to have information according to which there are reasonable grounds to suspect that person of having committed a crime. Given the way in which they separated these people, well, there were no controls. Nothing was checked. As far as I know, they had no evidence against those people, yet they were separated. And yet again, I'm claiming that it wouldn't have been a problem even if they had been separated. Had they been checked and if it wasn't shown that they had committed a crime, then they could have transported them somewhere. That wouldn't have been a problem. But my claim here is that most of those people were not members of the ABiH. Perhaps they were men who were fit for military service, but they were not members of that force. And I can say for certain that everyone who participated in a crime or war crime, everyone who killed civilian -- civilians, Serbs, or put fire to their property didn't arrive in Potocari. No one arrived in Potocari. Those who arrived in Potocari were people who certainly did not do anything and had no reason to flee across the forest. They went to Potocari to be safe with their families and to be evacuated to the liberated territory, which is what had been agreed. So that is my opinion as far as the -- as these people are concerned, the sort of people who were separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question from yesterday's transcript. This was at 24621, lines 24 and 25. You were talking about this process and how you thought that there would be some type of screening of the men, and you said: "That was my first thought when I heard about the separation. After that, of course, you know what happened." I just want to ask you what happened? What did you mean when you said "you know what happened," to all the men who had been separated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I wanted to say is that as someone from the security organ, I know what the security organ's duties in Potocari should have been. Military selection involves the sort of process I've mentioned earlier on. It involves identifying those who have committed a crime or those whom you suspect of having committed a crime, a war crime, or any other kind of crime, crime against the civilian population or against prisoners, soldiers, and so on and so forth. So I'm convinced that this is a legitimate military process that is done in all armies when dealing with prisoners, and naturally this screening concerns soldiers who surrenders to you and concerns individuals who may have committed crimes, so individuals that you suspect of having committed crimes. But no one else should be the subject of screenings, civilians who have nothing to do with the military. If you have no information on them, there is no need to separate them. When I mentioned those who were separated in Potocari, when I heard what Popovic was saying, I understood what was going to happen was what in fact happened, what we were discussing, but all those who remained in Potocari were separated. They were first detained in Potocari in houses, in certain facilities, and afterwards they were transferred to Bratunac, and they were detained in the primary school Vuk Karadzic, mostly in that school on the first day. And then what I know for sure is that these very same people, in the morning on the 14th, were transferred to the territory of Zvornik municipality, and all those who were separated in Potocari were temporarily detained, transferred to Bratunac and then to Zvornik, and after they'd been taken to Zvornik, they were executed in the territory of Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene for the transcript. In the first sentence, the witness said that when he heard Popovic speak, he thought that what was to ensue was what he described, which is the legitimate military screening, whereas we don't see that the way the first sentence is recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can you confirm what Mr. Karadzic said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't speak English. I cannot compare what I said with what's in the transcript. I can only repeat what I have stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said this: When I heard what Mr. Popovic said, it was my understanding that by going to Potocari a military screening process was to take place, which is a legitimate military procedure entailing identification -- the identification of those who need to be separated, and checks are carried out because there is a possibility of those who committed war crimes and crimes against humanity being present. That was my understanding, and that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and that is why I intervened for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, what is it that you heard from Mr. Popovic by when you say, "When I heard what Mr. Popovic said"? What word of Mr. Popovic did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Mr. Popovic, on the 12th in the morning, before the 10.00 meeting, said that the women and children were to go to Tuzla, to free territory, and that the military -- the men who are fit for military service would be separated in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to clarify this, yesterday at 24621 you said that Mr. Popovic also said, you've testified about this before, that all the men should be killed, and that after that there was a discussion of execution sites; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I have testified to that yesterday. He said that all Balijas should be killed. That's what I meant, and I didn't think I needed to explain again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Mr. Nikolic, if that is what Mr. Popovic said, how is it consistent with separating them and screening them? I meant screening them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to kill someone, that person must be separated from the rest of the group. In other words, the Muslims separated at Potocari were previously part of a group of 35.000 civilians. That was the context I tried to describe when the separation of men is concerned as well as the transport of women and children from Potocari. That is the context I was describing yesterday and today. Popovic was perfectly clear that in Potocari able-bodied men should be separated who were there. However, as I have explained yesterday, not only able-bodied men were separated but all men were separated in Potocari. All those who tried to board the buses, irrespective of whether they were able-bodied or not, it was enough that they were men and that's why they were separated. And all the separated men were Muslim. There was no one else there in Potocari. And when I asked him what would happen with the people, Mr. Popovic said that Balijas, referring to them, ought to be killed, every one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, after Popovic said that they should all be killed, you said there was a discussion as to the locations where they should be killed, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Who took part in those discussions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, Mr. Kosoric, and I participated in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one more clarification, because I wasn't clear about this. After having heard from Mr. Popovic that all men are to be killed, or all Balijas are to be killed, how could you think what would ensue is a legitimate military procedure entailing identification -- the identification of those who need to be separated and checks are carried out because there's a possibility of those who committed war crimes and crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've also answered similar questions before. At the moment when he said that, to be honest, I did not believe that all the men, all the Balijas in Potocari, would be killed. I have testified to that before. I believed then, and I couldn't even presume that things would develop the way they did. That was my belief. At the moment he said that all the Balijas should be killed, I thought that as many times before, because I heard many people, many officers say similar things, that Balijas should be killed or this or that, I thought this was yet another statement by Popovic who had the habit of saying things like that. So I thought that it wasn't exactly what he meant and that we would indeed do what was prescribed under the rules. However, things developed quite the other way following what he said, and what followed is what I have testified to before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But again, after Popovic said all the Balijas should be killed, there was a discussion of where these men could be executed, including Sase mine and Ciglana brick factory; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I leave it there. 65 ter 01947, please. While it's coming up, I'll say this is a document from RDB head Dragan Kijac, 13 July 1995, to the RS deputy minister of the interior personally and the head of the RS MUP Bijeljina RJB Public Security Department personally. First of all, do you know who the deputy minister of the interior was on 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew -- I think it was Mr. Kijac, or perhaps not. I'll think of the name later on. I can't off-the-cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was talking about the deputy minister of the interior. If you don't remember, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I even know him personally, but I can't recall his name. I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Tomo Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely. Tomo Kovac was either his deputy or acting in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You spoke yesterday about how state security -- that one of the separated men they took custody of was Mr. Mustafic. If we look at the first paragraph, first full paragraph of this document, we see it begins talking about the events of the night of 12-13 July, saying that members of the VRS and the MUP have started capturing large numbers of Muslim soldiers in ambushes set up in the general Konjevic Polje area. Further down it states: "The operation to detect and neutralise the Muslim troops is continuing. Earlier information regarding their intentions and the axis of movement towards Kladanj and Tuzla (Buljim-Pobudje-Konjevic Polje-Kaldrmica-Cerska-Snagovo-Crni Vrh) has been confirmed many times in interviews with prisoners." Now, very simply, is that just a reference to information that the security organs have learned from interrogating captured Muslim men, or separated Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is mostly intelligence information to the effect that in the period referred to -- well, we had that information at the command and as well as in the police structures at the time. In other words, my answer is yes, this is the intelligence information that was in use at the time at the level of army commands and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the bottom of that paragraph it states and it's written here: "Ibgan Mustafic, a former SDA deputy in the former BH Assembly and a great opponent of Naser Oric, was among the prisoners and can, with the necessary preparation, be used well in the media. " What I'm just asking you is: Is this the same man, the same Mustafic, that you referred to him as Ibran, that you discussed yesterday, had been taken into custody by state security?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ibran Mustafic, who was a SDA deputy in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender that document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be Exhibit P4389.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Moving on chronologically, Mr. Nikolic, I want to get to the 13th of July now. Is it correct that the night of the 12th to the -- into the 13th you were duty officer at the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. As of 7.00 on the 12th of July until 7.00 on the 13th of July; that is to say, 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd just like to go through the 13th of July, what you did that day, the places you went, the people you saw. Let's start off with the morning. Where did you go, what did you do first thing on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th -- or, rather, I was duty officer between the 12th and the 13th. At around 3.00 on the 13th, 3.00 a.m., that is, I went to sleep. I slept for an hour or two. And at around 7.00 I was back at the Bratunac Brigade command. I was there first in the morning at around 9.00 or 9.30. There was a meeting at the command attended by General Ratko Mladic, Colonel Vasic of the police, General Krstic, Popovic, my commander, as well as a number of other officers. I wasn't present at the meeting, and I don't know what it is that they discussed. Before I had a hand-over of duty the meeting took place. Following the meeting, I spoke with my commander in his office, and he told me that on the 13th, I was to continue with my activities of the 12th, which is basically the area of Potocari and the operation that was underway there. Having concluded that conversation with him, I went to Potocari where I saw that, much as the previous day, the transport of people who were there resumed. I saw and was in contact with Dusko Jevic of the MUP special brigade. I told him then -- so it's the 13th. By that time we already had information that on the road between Konjevic Polje, Sandici, Pervani, and Kaldrmica, as well Nova Kasaba, people were already surrendering and that many Muslim soldiers and civilians were being captured. I said that if he was in radio contact with the units, the police units, along that route to tell them that all those who surrendered or were captured be transferred to the facilities designated for detaining those who were captured. After a short stay in Potocari, I returned to the Bratunac Brigade command. I went to the seat of the military police. Mirko Jankovic, the MP commander, told me that on that day, the 13th, along the road Bratunac-Kravica-Konjevic Polje and further afield, Ratko Mladic was to travel there together with his team. The MP commander also told me that the unit of the Bratunac Brigade military police, which was escorting and securing General Mladic from the moment of his arrival, was to accompany him further and that they will continue to act as his security detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then we can continue on that trip. You referred to at the morning meeting on the 13th, which you did not attend, Colonel Vasic of the police. Is that Dragomir Vasic of the Zvornik centre?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Dragomir Vasic from Zvornik, chief of centre in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also explained to us that when you spoke with Dusko Jevic, this is on page 18 at lines 15, if he was in radio contact with the units, the police unit, along the route to tell them that all those who surrendered or were captured be transferred to the facilities designated for detaining those who were captured. My question is: Were these men who were captured along the road, were they going to be treated the same way as the men separated in Potocari, detained in the same facilities in Bratunac, or was there something different about the way these captured men were going to be processed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know of any other or different intention. All those separated in Potocari and all those captured along the route had the same status. I don't know of any other or different treatment or intentions. As far as I know, all the men were treated the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd interrupted you, and you were starting to tell us how you learned that General Mladic was in the vicinity and was going to be travelling along the Bratunac-Kravica-Konjevic Polje road. So can you just tell us what you did with Mirko Jankovic in regard to Ratko Mladic's security.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards General Ratko Mladic's route, it is an obligation on the security organ that for as long as the commander of the Main Staff, Ratko Mladic, was in Bratunac in the AOR of my unit, it was my obligation, in addition to undertaking additional security measures, which he otherwise enjoyed in terms of immediate security as well as the additional military police detachment from our unit. On top of all that, I was under an obligation to verify security situation along the route he was to travel at any given point in time. On this occasion, I took a military policeman, and we went together by vehicle to the road itself between Kravica and Konjevic Polje. I wanted to check the safety of the road and whether any traffic could move along. I had information that by that time there were already police forces deployed along the route. In any case, I wanted to see it for myself. At around 12.00, perhaps, I set off from Bratunac and arrived in Konjevic Polje some half an hour later at an intersection or a crossroads which takes one to Bratunac, Vlasenica, or Zvornik, and the crossroads is called Konjevic Polje. If you want me to tell you what things I saw along the route, I can tell you. There were police forces there by that time at Sandici. The special brigade was deployed. They were easy to identify. They had heavy weaponry, APCs, and a tank. En route, I also saw Mr. Borovcanin in Sandici where the heavy weaponry was deployed. Further along the route there was nothing in particular on my way there as opposed to on my way back. Once in Konjevic Polje, I saw something I had already known, which is that there was a check-point manned by the police. It was manned by the men of the public security station from Bratunac. The policemen were at the check-point in Konjevic Polje, and it was a permanent check-point even before the operation began and Srebrenica fell. I waited there for some 40, 45 minutes when General Mladic appeared. He arrived in Konjevic Polje, parked in front of an old yellow building which is there no longer on the right-hand side as one entered Konjevic Polje. His security detail came out as well, as well as the military policemen of the Bratunac Brigade. I reported to him that the road was safe, and it was an official military report, which is something I was obliged to do upon his arrival. Do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Let me ask you, on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, on the trip to Konjevic Polje, in addition to the MUP forces you've described, did you see any prisoners on the way to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that on the first occasion in Sandici there were some prisoners. They had surrendered in Sandici. There was a group of about 10 or 15 people who had already surrendered, and they were at that place in Sandici where Ljubisa Borovcanin was also present. So on that first occasion, I don't remember there being a large number of imprisoned individuals at some other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At Konjevic Polje, were there prisoners when you saw General Mladic there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a slightly higher number of people who had surrendered in Konjevic Polje or who had been captured. Some people were in Konjevic Polje in a facility in a meadow at the crossroads itself, or not too far from the cross roads, in fact, and some of the prisoners were somewhere in a house or in a facility that belonged to the 5th Engineers Battalion, and that's where they had been provided with accommodation and where security was being organised for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you see whether General Mladic had any interaction with the prisoners? Did he speak to them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After he got out of the car, after I had reported to him, he approached those people in the meadow at the crossroads in Konjevic Polje, and he addressed them and said, and I paraphrase, Don't worry. Everything will be fine. There won't be any problems. He addressed them very briefly. He promised that nothing would happen to them. He said that they would be transferred to where they wanted to go, and that was the essence of what he said to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you heard that? You heard him saying those words?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because I was with him all the time. I was by his side or right behind him. So I was with him all the time that he was in Konjevic Polje, because those are the military rules, or wherever he went, I went too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you have any discussion with General Mladic after he gave those reassuring words to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to General Mladic after he had finished speaking to them and went to the place where his car was parked. At that point in time I asked him something. I said, General, what's going to happen to these people? That was my question. And General Mladic didn't reply. He just looked at me and gestured with his hand in this manner. He then smiled and got into the car. So that was his reaction. He didn't make any comments of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just for our record, the gesture he made was kind of sweeping at his waist with his right hand from the left to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, after that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you heard the answer, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The question is: Mr. Nikolic, is that correct the way I described the gesture? Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we need your verbal answer for the benefit of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I showed you what I saw. There was no comment. General Mladic didn't say anything, so I showed you the gesture he made with his hand. It was a gesture with his hand from the left to the right, and that's more or less what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened next, and specifically I'm asking if you met a man named Resid Sinanovic about this time and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Konjevic Polje, after the meeting -- or, rather, after General Mladic had left and went his way, members of the police told me that they had an important prisoner. When I asked who it was, they told me that it was Resid Sinanovic. Do you want me to tell you what then happened, or will you put questions to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll -- I'll put the question. What -- did you meet Mr. Sinanovic, and what did you do next? Where did you take him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I had been provided with that information, the military policemen and myself took charge of Resid Sinanovic. The civilian police delivered him into our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was he before the war? What is his position and -- I'll ask that first.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resid Sinanovic was, among other things, the chief of the public security station in Bratunac before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you know why he was considered -- the MUP who had custody of him, why did they consider him an important prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only make an assumption. The chief of the public security station in a small town, that's an important person. Resid Sinanovic was important probably for another reason, too, because before the war he held high positions in the MUP, inter alia, and the reason why he was taken over was the fact that Resid Sinanovic was on that list of persons from Bratunac who were considered to be -- or, rather, there was reasonable doubt that he had committed war crimes during the war. That's why he was an important prisoner, and that's why I took him over as a man who was a war crimes suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where did you deliver him to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I brought Sinanovic to Bratunac, and I personally handed him over to Zlatan Celanovic. That is the person that I told you about yesterday, that I testified about yesterday. So he was a law -- lawyer who was in charge of interrogating suspects, and also then criminal charges were supposed to be brought against individuals and then this person would be prosecuted by the appropriate authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you find out from Zlatan Celanovic whether he interviewed Mr. Sinanovic and whether he found that he -- that there was cause to prosecute him as a criminal?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zlatan Celanovic had a duty, and that was the standing practice in my brigade; that is to say, after dealing with each detainee, prisoner, each person who was brought in, the results of the interview or the report involved should be submitted to the commander and to myself. This time, Zlatan Celanovic, I think even on the very same day when I brought him -- or perhaps the next day, in the morning, informed me that on the basis of everything that he had, on the basis of all the statements, on the basis of what he heard from Sinanovic during the interview, that he believed that there were no grounds for keeping him any longer and that there was no reason to bring criminal charges against him or to file an indictment. That's what he said to me at his own initiative. He made that decision at his own initiative after some Serbs from Bratunac who were his friends who used to work with him came to visit Sinanovic, and after that visit he decided to transfer Resid Sinanovic to the Vuk Karadzic school where all the other prisoners were kept. And according to the information I have, that is where he was transferred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And briefly, to the best of your knowledge, what happened to Resid Sinanovic after he was transferred to the Vuk Karadzic school on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After he was transferred to where the other prisoners were, this is what I know: On the 14th, in the morning, within the convoy that went to Zvornik, Resid Sinanovic left together with all the other prisoners who were in the Vuk Karadzic school and at the other buildings in Bratunac. Now, in Zvornik, I don't know. I have no information. In Zvornik, like all others, he was executed, shot dead, brought out to be executed. And then I heard that he was wounded, and although wounded, he swam across the Drina River. That is the river that is a natural boundary between Bosnia and Serbia. He swam to the other bank and reached a restaurant in Banja Koviljaca, a small place there. People recognise many him because they're neighbours and Sinanovic often went there. They recognised him and they transferred him to a hospital. Everything that happened after that and everything that has to do with his medical treatment, my lawyers investigated that. They took the medical documents that had to do with his treatment in hospital. I think that later he was transferred to Loznica, but there is this complete documentation that my lawyers handed over to the OTP. A lady doctor who worked in the hospital there was his neighbour from Bratunac. So when the war started, from the Bratunac health centre she went to Loznica and worked as a doctor there. She recognised him. Then also -- I mean, they lived on the same floor in this apartment buildings, so they literally lived next door, a metre away from each other. She called the station in Bratunac. She informed them about this, and they probably, I assume, informed the centre or the police in Zvornik, and according to the information I have, the police, the civilian police, took him over in Loznica. I'm saying this only on the basis of this information. I mean, I don't have any reliable information. I'm just telling you about the information that I heard. The police who took him over killed him on the bridge between Zvornik and Serbia, in that area. That is what I know about that particular case. My lawyers directly investigated all of this, and there is documentation concerning his stay and medical treatment in Banja Koviljaca and Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the purpose of scheduling, although I'm not sure whether we can sit until 3.00 today, but the first break will be at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we can go chronologically through the rest of 13 July. After you delivered Mr. Sinanovic to Zlatan Celanovic, I believe you made another trip out towards Konjevic Polje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said yes, that's right. I went once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why did you go out again this time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went once again with the commander of the military police and with the deputy, with Mirko Jankovic and Mile Petrovic. In the brigade command we had a few APCs from the Dutch Battalion. Mirko Jankovic knew how to drive a APC, so we went there because at that point in time that is where everything was happening, everything that had to do with combat, prisoner-taking, and so on. So from Potocari the focus moved to that area, Kravica, Konjevic Polje, Kasaba. So I went there. Mirko Jankovic took that APC, the commander of the military police. Mile and I got into the APC and went to Mirko, to that area, together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did that APC have a loudspeaker, some kind of broadcast system?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the APCs that were there had loudspeakers as part of their regular equipment. In addition to other things, they had loudspeakers too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in your previous answer, we heard the translation that "Mile and I got into the APC and went to Mirko, to that area, together." Could you clarify that, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that that's what I said. Well, possibly. So Mirko Jankovic knew how to drive an APC. He took this APC. Mirko Jankovic drove it, and Mile Petrovic and I entered that APC, and together with Mirko Jankovic we went to the area of Bratunac-Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you -- was that loudspeaker used on the trip, and, if so, what was it used for?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mile Petrovic, after Kravica, roughly from the village of Sandici and further on, that is to say towards Konjevic Polje, used that loudspeaker, and from time to time, I mean the APC was moving slowly, he called upon the Muslims to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did any Muslim men surrender to you and Mirko and -- Mirko Jankovic and Mile Petrovic? Did you take any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the sake of the truth, I have to say that I'm not sure now whether what you want me to say was a consequence of the call over the loudspeaker. Now, whether somebody surrendered because Mile Petrovic was calling them to surrender, I cannot say that that's the way it was, and I cannot deny it either, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you again and ask the question, okay, because maybe it was mis-interpreted. I didn't talk about the process and there's nothing I want you to say other than what you remember. Let me ask you the question again. Did any Muslim men surrender to you? Did you take any prisoners? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that can be defined as surrender, I will explain what happened and then we can discuss whether that is surrender. So along the road towards Konjevic Polje, Mirko Jankovic, Mile Petrovic, and I were in this APC, and along this road we caught up with six Muslims who were moving towards Konjevic Polje. We stopped the APC. We stopped it, and we took them into the APC. That is the absolute truth. That is what happened. We took them into the APC and drove them to Konjevic Polje. That's what happened. There was no fighting. Surrender is something that you force people to do. That's what I think. They did not offer any resistance. They did not attack us. They did not shoot at us. We did not shoot at them. We quite simply took them into this APC and drove them to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for explaining the way that worked. What happened at Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second time -- or, rather, when I returned to Konjevic Polje, in Konjevic Polje, indeed there was already a large number of prisoners who had already been taken prisoner, between 250 and 300 people, roughly, in one area. In another area, there were, say, 10 or 15 people. So in this area, people, Muslims were surrendering en masse already. As we arrived in Konjevic Polje, Mirko Jankovic parked the APC there and I said to Mile Petrovic, Mile, please, these people who are in the APC, take them there together with this group that is already there. After I said that to him, I went -- say, 50 metres away from the crossroads there's a burned house, and I sat underneath part of that burned house. There were five or six Muslims there, and they were even roasting something there. There was a fire there, and there was the civilian police, there were these Muslims, and I sat on this slab of concrete that was there. After a while, I heard a burst of gunfire that could be heard from some place that was very, very close. After this burst of gunfire, perhaps five or six minutes later, Mile Petrovic showed up and addressed me with the following words: Boss, today I revenged my brother. And I said, What did you do? And he said, I killed him. That was the conversation between myself and him. I did not ask him anything. To be quite frank, I didn't even know that his brother was killed. I mean, quite simply, I did not make any comments. I did not ask him anything else. After that they went towards Kuslat with this APC, and that was the entire conversation, the dialogue between him and me as far as the fate of these six men is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if it is convenient, shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's one matter I'd like to deal with before we break. I can say it in public session. Mr. Robinson, in light of yesterday's filing by Germany, the Chamber is of the view that before it starts considering your motion to report Germany to the Security Council, the best way to proceed would be for you to set up another interview and see how that plays out. Also, I note that Germany's offering you the option of providing the German authorities with written questions for Mr. von Bezolt. This may be worth considering by you and your team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to introduce Kirsten Schelwitz, who is from the United States and working as an intern with our case managers. She will be joining us this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I now confirm that we will be sitting until 3.00 today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, before we move on, just a couple questions, Mr. Nikolic. Do you know a man named Nenad Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was -- what was his position, or what unit, if any, or group was he a member of in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1995, he was a policeman at the public security station in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995, he was also a policeman, but -- or, rather, he was in the unit at the check-point in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about a man named Mirko Petro -- Peric? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know Mirko Peric personally, too. Mirko Peric was a policeman as well. He belonged to the public security station Bratunac. On that day, the 13th, when I was in Konjevic Polje, I saw Mirko Peric as well at the check-point in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be very clear, as well as, you mean you saw him as well as Nenad Deronjic at the check-point in Konjevic Polje on 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. After this trip to Konjevic Polje which you've described to us, did you return to Bratunac that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I returned on the same day, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened when you returned to Bratunac in the evening? Who did you meet? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned to Bratunac, I went to the command of my brigade. I think I was in the kitchen when I was informed from the communications centre that I should report to Bratunac, to Colonel Beara. After dinner, say between 8.00 and 8.30 p.m. on that day, I went and met up with Colonel Beara in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the time. In your previous testimony in the Tolimir case, at 12409 is the page, you said that it was around 5.30 or 6.00 p.m. that you were told in the communications centre to meet with Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I ever said anything even similar to that. The interpretation I heard was that I met with Colonel Beara at the communications centre. I never stated that, but that is the interpretation I heard just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's wrong. That's not what I said. Let me ask it again. I'm just trying to talk about the timing. In your previous testimony, you said that you were told at about 5.30 or 6.00 p.m. that you should meet with Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the time when I returned to the Bratunac Brigade from Konjevic Polje and that is correct, that is to say in that period, but then, again, every time I testify I say this. I do not want to specify exact times because it's been so many years. I really can no longer remember whether it was an hour or half an hour here or there. At any rate, I can speak specifically and precisely about with a happened about events, but this is tentatively the time when I returned from Konjevic Polje. I went to eat in the kitchen, and that is when I received this information from the communications centre that I should report to Colonel Beara. That is correct, and that is what I testified to every time, and I confirm it this time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And did you meet with Colonel -- you say you went up and you met with Colonel Beara in town. Tell us what happened then.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met up with him. Colonel Beara ordered me, told me, whatever you wish, but I think that this is a kind of order, to go to the command of the Zvornik Brigade to find Drago Nikolic, the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade, and to convey to him his order to have facilities prepared as well as people for providing security and to convey to him the decision that the prisoners who are in Bratunac would be transferred to the zone of the Zvornik Brigade and that conditions should be provided for taking them in, detaining them, and that there should be physical security provided for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did Colonel Beara order you to inform Drago [Realtime transcript read in error "Dragan"] Nikolic about anything else that would happen to the prisoners once they reached the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Beara and I spoke very briefly. I told you what the essence of that was. Then on the 13th, I already had information, meaning I already knew on the evening of the 13th what would happen to these people who had been taken prisoner. It wasn't necessary to say anything directly, but from the conversation with him, I did understand that that was the message roughly of Colonel Beara, that these people who were going down there would be executed in the territory of the municipality of Zvornik. However, I can say that already then -- actually, the situation was clear as regards their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, your question at line 5, "Dragan Nikolic" should read "Drago Nikolic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want you to be a little bit more precise if you can. You said, It wasn't necessary to say anything directly, but from the conversation with him, I did understand that that was the message roughly of Colonel Beara, that these people who were going down there would be executed in the territory of the Zvornik Brigade. Now, did Colonel Beara order you to convey to Drago Nikolic that the men would be executed in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, really, I cannot. I mean, I always have this dilemma when I testify about that, but I think -- it's not that I think. As far as I can remember -- actually, when he ordered me to go to Zvornik, among other things he said that these people should be transferred down there and that they would be killed in Zvornik. However, the dilemma I've had all of these years is that I do not remember exactly the way in which he communicated that to me. I cannot be specific there. However, what I understood and what I conveyed to Drago was -- I mean, my understanding was that these people were being transferred there in order to be killed in Zvornik. That was my understanding. That was the message that I did convey to Drago when I saw him. What I knew was that these people would be transferred and killed in the territory of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could briefly describe for us the trip to Zvornik and how you met up with Drago Nikolic and conveyed this information.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After I received the order I got into the car and drove to Zvornik. The trip to Zvornik took about an hour and 15 minutes. It's 40, 42, 45 kilometres to the brigade command. I reached the HQ of the Zvornik Brigade, went to the reception and asked to be taken to see Draga [as interpreted] Nikolic. The soldiers at the reception assigned a soldier to me who escorted me to a room in the Zvornik Brigade command. I arrived there, and in the office I met an officer. I told him that I needed to contact Drago Nikolic directly. I sat down there, and two or three minutes later he called an officer, a man who came to the office. He asked me whether he could help me since Drago Nikolic wasn't there. I said that my orders were that I should convey the order directly to Drago Nikolic, and I said that what I had to convey to him could not be said to him. Afterwards, the officer in the room told the policeman, ordered the policeman, in fact, to escort me to the forward command post, and I was told that Drago Nikolic was there, that he was the duty officer there. I was told that the policeman would escort me there. We left the command. We got into my car, and first we drove down the asphalt road and then down the macadam road to the place. I arrived there, parked in front of the house where the command post of theirs was located. The policeman entered the house, called to Drago Nikolic, then came back out, and my conversation with Drago Nikolic took five, six, seven, ten minutes at the most, and I told him that I had been sent there by Colonel Beara for a certain reason. I told him what the reason was. I conveyed the order to him, and then I told Drago that I had information according to which the people who were going to his area would be killed in Zvornik. Drago Nikolic didn't make any comments. He said, I'm the duty officer, I'll contact my command, and then I will see what action should be taken. At the door with Drago Nikolic there was a communications officer, and afterwards the policeman and myself got back into the car and returned to Zvornik. I left the policeman in Zvornik and continued my trip to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Had you met Drago Nikolic before this night?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Drago Nikolic in private capacity. He is from my village. I had no meetings with Drago Nikolic. Never. Perhaps we had seen each other one or two occasions at the most, but over those days, no, I didn't meet or speak to Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right, but my question was just more simple. That wasn't the first time you'd met Drago Nikolic that night. Had you met him before?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That question is different to the one I answered. I know Drago from before, and that was not the first time that I had met Drago. Yes, I know Drago from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on -- you continued, you said, your trip to Bratunac. Did you see any buses heading towards Zvornik area as you were going back towards Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was returning to Bratunac, the Kuslata sector, the village of Kuslat, I saw three or four buses heading in the direction of Zvornik. They were full of people who were going to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you have any information of whether prisoners, Muslim men prisoners from Bratunac were taken to Zvornik at about this time? Is that the same buses or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The buses that I have just mentioned are buses which were heading towards Zvornik from Konjevic Polje, Konjevic Polje-Drinjaca-Zvornik. When I arrived in Bratunac in the evening, on the 13th in the evening, from the command of the military police and of the police I was told that a convoy of Muslims, five or six buses, as far as I can remember, I was told that such a convoy had taken a different route which also led in the direction of Zvornik. It's Bratunac, the bridge over the Drina-Polim-Zelinje-Drinjaca-Zvornik direction. So that is the road that leads to Zvornik along the Drina River. It's the old road towards Zvornik. It's not an asphalted road but it was a practicable route that could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for at that clarification. Now, when you returned back to Bratunac that night, what was the situation in town?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to Bratunac around 12.00. At the time, the situation in Bratunac was terrible. It was chaotic. Those are the right terms to use. There were many problems. The situation was such that it was very difficult to control anything under such conditions. It was very difficult to organise anything under such conditions. When I arrived in Bratunac, at that time all the facilities for detention were more or less full in the town, in all the streets from the centre of the town. From the municipality building in Bratunac and onwards, none of the roads, none of the roads, the main roads or the side roads were empty. There were buses or lorries parked in those roads. The football stadium, for example, the parking places, a kilometre and a half outside the town on the periphery, you could also find buses and lorries with people who had been brought in from the direction of Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje. The situation was chaotic, and that is putting it mildly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, when you're talking about these buses and lorries, people brought in, these are prisoners, Muslim men prisoners; correct, held on those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole -- well, in fact, not on the whole, but in a hundred per cent of those cases, all those who were in the buses and in the lorries were prisoners who had been captured on those axes, and on the 13th in the evening hours and in the course of the night, they were transferred to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where else were prisoners held in Bratunac that night on the 13th, besides buses and lorries?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, on that night they were also kept in the Vuk Karadzic primary school in the physical training hall of that very same primary school, in a hangar as well. And, also, as far as I know, another school was made use of. It's the old school, the secondary Djuro Pucar school. It's an old building that was there before the war, and it was the secondary school in Bratunac until a new school was built. And in those facilities there were these prisoners who were being held there. They had been separated in Potocari or they had subsequently been transferred from Konjevic Polje and Kasaba to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about the playground or stadium?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, a few buses were parked in the direction of the stadium and in the area immediately after the entry; but if you're referring to the pitch itself, as far as I know, there were no prisoners there. There were buses, but the prisoners were in the buses, and in that part of the stadium, but in the stadium itself, on the pitch, in fact, there was no one according to the information I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At this point in time, around midnight, the night of the 13th of July, who was guarding these prisoners? Who was securing them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say the following: I can refer to the buildings. Perhaps that will be the best description of what was taking place there. The security for the Vuk Karadzic school was provided by part of the MPs from the Bratunac Brigade and also members of the public security station in Bratunac. As for the other facilities, the hangar, the physical training room, and the secondary school, the security was provided on the whole by the police from various formations, units. Police from the public security station in Bratunac or policemen from special purposes units or there were even policemen from the special companies, these companies from special brigades, they provided security in the evening hours. I don't know how this worked exactly, but I know that the military police, members of the military police, members of the civilian police from various structures were providing security. There were also soldiers who provided security and civilians to whom weapons had been distributed since there weren't enough people for security. So they would provide security for the buses and the lorries for these vehicles that had been brought into Bratunac. So on the whole, everyone who was available and who could be engaged participated in addition to those whose task it was to provide security, and it was their task to provide security for the Muslims who had been taken to Bratunac in buses or in lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you hear whether any prisoners were killed during that night in any of the detention facilities in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all this came to an end, after a certain period of time had passed, when speaking to Dragan Mirkovic I found out that on that evening, between the 13th and the 14th, people were killed in the hangar, mostly in the hangar, and also in the physical training hall, the sports hall. As far as the Vuk Karadzic primary school is concerned, according to my information there were no killings, but in the hangar and in the sports hall in the Vuk Karadzic primary school people were taken out and killed. In addition to those cases in which people were killed, I had information according to which certain individuals were taken out and certain people were killed in revenge. Serbs whose family members had been killed wanted to find Muslims according to -- they wanted to find Muslims who had allegedly kill members of their family. I had evidence about such killings -- or, rather, I had evidence from -- about individuals who had taken Muslims out of buses in order to kill them for purposes of revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You've described the situation that night, and you'd started telling us that you were told to meet Colonel Beara. Where did you meet -- well, what happened next? Did you meet with Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I've understood the question correctly, did I meet Colonel Beara? Well, I have already spoken about the meeting and about what happened. If the question is whether I met Colonel Beara after the return from Zvornik, well, in that case that's a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Having returned from Zvornik, as I've already said, I returned about 12.00. I went to the Fontana Hotel which is where Colonel Beara was, and I gave a report to Colonel Beara. I told him that I had gone to Zvornik and I had carried out his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I had told him that I had carried out his orders, Colonel Beara asked me to take him to the SDS office in Bratunac, and naturally it's not far from the Fontana Hotel to the SDS office. We got up, left the Fontana Hotel and set off in the direction of the SDS office. I arrived there and when I enter the office, Miroslav Deronjic and Colonel Vasic were already there. I arrived can Colonel Beara and we entered those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, this is Dragomir Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Dragomir Vasic, the chief of the centre. He was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we entered the premises, and I have to say this for the benefit of the Chamber, these premises consist of two offices. One of the offices is an office in which there's a desk and a number of chairs, and the other office is a small reception area. There was a small table and a couple of chairs as well. I arrived with Colonel Beara. Miroslav Deronjic was in the office. I told Miroslav Deronjic, This is my boss from the Main Staff, Colonel Beara, and I entered that room. I sat down in the reception area. In between the reception area and Deronjic's office, well, there was just a distance of about a metre and a metre and a half between those two offices, so there's a very small area there. And at the very beginning they started discussing things, and they started quarreling. Colonel Beara said that he had received instructions from his boss as to what should be done with the prisoners, and Miroslav Deronjic referred to the instructions he had received from his boss, President Karadzic. He said he had instructions from his boss regarding what was to be done with the prisoners. For the sake of informing the Trial Chamber, I have to explain something because I know this is contradictory, but I'm telling you exactly what happened. Colonel Beara sent me to Zvornik to say that the prisoners would be going to Zvornik. This happened when I arrived in the centre and received orders. And when I arrived in the SDS office, Colonel Beara insisted at that meeting that those prisoners should remain in Bratunac. Why was this happening? Well, since I was the duty officer on the 12th and I know exactly how the information was distributed and how orders were given, well, on the 13th the decisions taken, especially on the 13th, changed rapidly. So first you would receive one order and half an hour later the order was amended, you would receive a different order, and that was the situation that prevailed in Bratunac at the time, and in particular on the 13th when there were many problems. Miroslav Deronjic was insistent and he said that he had received instructions according to which all prisoners in Bratunac should be transferred to Zvornik. First they quarreled. They confronted -- they had a confrontation of opinions, and then they sat down at the table. Miroslav took out some glasses, put alcohol into the glasses and had a drink and continued to speak to each other. I have testified to this previously. On the 13th in the evening at about 12.00 or between 12.00 and half past 12.00 when this meeting was being held, the status or the fate of the prisoners was certain, and no one no longer asked about what should be done with the prisoners. It was openly said that these prisoners would be killed. The only issue was whether these prisoners should be killed in Bratunac or in Zvornik. That was the dilemma. That was the subject of the dispute. Miroslav Deronjic insisted that he had a sufficient number of problems in Bratunac. He said he didn't want anyone to be killed in Bratunac. And that is why he was insistent. And finally they reached an agreement. At the end of the meeting everyone, agreed that the prisoners should be transferred to Zvornik or to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade in the coming days. In addition to these issues that were discussed, a number of other issues were discussed, issues that concerned dealing with the current problems in Bratunac. These issues concerned providing security for the prisoners. They concerned the threat if they came out of the buses or the lorries, the risk. So these were the security issues that were discussed and that they attempted to deal with that evening. So in brief, that is what happened at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, sir. I just want to be extremely clear. You've testified about this before. What did Miroslav Deronjic say his instructions were that he had received from President Karadzic regarding the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic claimed that he had received instructions according to which all prisoners from Bratunac should leave Bratunac in the following days. That is what Miroslav Deronjic insisted on. He said, I have received instructions from President Karadzic according to which the prisoners in Bratunac should be transferred to Zvornik, and Deronjic then said that he did not want anyone to be killed in Bratunac. He said he had enough problems as it was and he didn't want this. That's what I heard in relation to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. Nikolic, your previous evidence, testimony, is not in evidence in this case. So probably you may have to repeat, but what did Beara insist upon? I'm not sure whether you talked about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beara was at the meeting and at half past 8.00 he had issued orders to me, but it was different later. He said everyone would be transferred to Zvornik. I should tell Drago Nikolic about that. But at that meeting he insisted that these soldiers should remain in Bratunac. It differed from his previous order. That is what I was telling you about, because I know that there is a difference. I know that it is contradictory. He was insisting, first of all, that they should remain in Bratunac and then -- or, rather, at the first meeting, he insisted that they should go to Zvornik; and at the second meeting, he insisted on them remaining in Bratunac. So this is contradictory. All I want to do is tell you the truth about what happened. I know that this is contradictory, but it's the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene. In line 18, it says "contradictory." Later the witness said the one excludes the other, and that wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say that Beara told you that these soldiers should remain in Bratunac? Did he use the term "soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
