utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prisoners. Prisoners. Perhaps it was a slip of the tongue. I'm referring to the prisoners who were in Bratunac. Among the prisoners, there were soldiers, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that prisoners and captives doesn't mean the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because we heard "soldiers." Yes, please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You've explained that the agreement was reached in the end between the parties present. What happened next? What did you do after this, after what you've finished telling us what happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, it was late. I went to the Bratunac Brigade command, and in the command of the Bratunac Brigade the colleagues of mine in the operations room and others who were present, and I told all of them that we all had to work up until the early morning hours, and I told them that I had information according to which these captives and everyone in Bratunac, all the Muslims, should be transferred to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade in the following days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let's move to the following day, 14 July. Tell us what happened with the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, in keeping with what had been arranged the previous evening, during the morning buses began arriving for the most part, although there were some trucks as well. In any case, in the column that was formed, there were trucks which came from that direction, and those who were already on those trucks remained there and simply joined the column. In the early hours of the 14th -- or, in the morning of the 14th, all those who were held in detention buildings and facilities entered the buses and boarded the trucks. The column was headed by an APC driven by Mirko Jankovic, MP platoon commander. The convoy was about 1 or 1.5 kilometres in length. It included all those who were captured on the 12th, as well as those taken prisoner and brought to Bratunac on the 13th. All of them went to the AOR of the Zvornik Brigade on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you know, can you tell us if you know at all about escorts, guards, of these transports, which -- whether there was military police, MUP, Bratunac Brigade, or who provided the escort to the prisoner convoy on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The escort of the convoy, that is to say the buses and trucks and all the people on them, resembled any similar security detail. Some of the military policemen who were available were included, as well as members of the civilian police. It also included those who had guarded the trucks that were outside the facilities. So it included members of the military police, civilian police, soldiers, and even civilians who stood guard and had weapons. They all escorted those they had guarded the previous night. That was how the escort was organised. The column was headed by an APC driven by the military police commander and the APC belonged to DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on now a little bit and talk about an issue that came up a few days later, past the 14th, and that's about the question of local staff of UNPROFOR and international organisations from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 02123, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, that's not a very good copy, but I think you're familiar with this document. It's from the command, the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade intelligence organ dated 18 July 1995, situation in the Srebrenica region. If we can go to the bottom of both documents, please. And to the left for the Serbian version. Can you see your name there on the bottom, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is there another page in the Serbian in e-court? Could we go to that if there is one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There's a handwritten copy of the same document, sir. Can you tell us about why there's two versions of this, a handwritten document and a teleprinter or typed version?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to correct you. There are no two versions. There is a single version. This is how all such documents were sent. You, an operative, sending the report writes it by hand, sends it to the communications centre. They type it out and send it on. Then you receive your handwritten version and the typed version back. That was standard procedure in submitting reports to your superior command or whoever was to receive such a report. This report was specific, though. I said yesterday that in my office there was Colonel Jankovic from the intelligence administration of the Main Staff. The two of us usually sent all information to our superior commands together. In practical terms, it meant once we had enough information, we sat down and made a draft of what we wanted to report about. This is not my handwriting. Colonel Jankovic wrote this report by hand, and after he did that, I took it and since it was the headquarters of my brigade, I took it to communication -- to the communications centre to be sent. This was done automatically. The person in the communications centre typed it out and sent it on, including my name on the report. So you have Colonel Jankovic's text with me in the signature block. That's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clear explanation. If we look at the bottom of this document -- we need to go to the next page of the Serbian, please. There's a question about local staff and the international organisations, and it says: "Will you please tell me what stand to take in terms of authorisation for evacuation of the international organisation Medecins sans Frontieres, in fact, how to deal with so-called local staff. This also applies to the interpreters of military monitors and UNPROFOR. RDB, regional state security, passed on to us an opinion that President Karadzic had allegedly abolished all local staff who used to work for UNPROFOR. It is our opinion that they should not be held." But first of all, what was the issue here about local staff? What does that mean, "local staff," of international organisations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "local staff" of international organisations, including DutchBat, because they, too, had people working for them from the local community of Srebrenica, this included for the most part all technical personnel; first and foremost, people in charge of maintenance such as plumbers, electricians, mechanics and different types of tradesmen who worked on either maintaining their buildings or their technical assets. When we brought this question up, we had those people in mind who worked with UNPROFOR, the ICRC, the MSF, the UNHCR, and -- am I forgetting anyone? Yes, and the military observers. They were Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave, and we asked what to do with them. Here you see what the position was and that we believed they shouldn't be held but, rather, allowed to leave with those who employed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just this sentence: "RDB passed on to us" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Should we ask the witness to read that sentence? Could you read out the last sentence for us, starting from "RDB."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hmm. "RDB conveyed to us the position that allegedly President Karadzic pardoned all local personnel working for UNPROFOR. It is our opinion that they shouldn't be held."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's helpful. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An intervention for the transcript. The witness said that the international observers, too, had such personnel, so does it include the international observers or only the local staff working for them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I completely object. I ask that you cut this off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is not a translation issue, it is not a appropriate moment for you to intervene, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the last sentence you read out, can you -- when you wrote this -- or, excuse me, when Colonel -- when Jankovic wrote it and then it was sent off, what is the meaning of that that President Karadzic has abolished or pardoned all local staff, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now do you hear me, Mr. Nikolic? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again, Mr. Nikolic. I'm sorry you didn't hear it the first time. When this last sentence that you read out was written by Jankovic and then it was sent out, what's the meaning? What did you understand that to mean, that President Karadzic had allegedly abolished or pardoned local staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure what it is that you want me to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, let me explain. When you read out, it was translated in English as "Mr. Karadzic allegedly pardoned all local staff," but in the English translation, in written form, it says, "Mr. Karadzic had allegedly abolished all local staff." I do not know the difference in B/C/S between "pardon" and "abolish," but that's the origin of confusion. Do you have any observation, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is absolutely clear now what the problem is. Without going into any explanations as to what "pardon" or "amnesty" mean in my country, I will say this: In my language, this means to me that the RDB sent information that Mr. Karadzic let them go free. In other words, that they should not be held and that they should not be separated. If it were the other way around, they would not have been allowed to leave with UNPROFOR or those they worked for. They would have been separated. That is one thing I wanted to say. Due to language differences, I wanted to also say this: In my country, where I live -- well, this was written by Colonel Jankovic. The term "to pardon" in the Serbian language, well, for that, one would have to have been sentenced first in order to be pardoned, but these people were not, so no pardon was necessary. They only needed to be permitted to leave the territory of the enclave together with those they worked for. There was no need for any pardon, because they had not been sentenced. They were simply employees of international organisations. Perhaps this clarifies things. If you require any further explanations, do ask. In any case, it does not mean what was in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4390, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you about now, sir, is what you can tell us about any operation that you know of to move the bodies of Muslim persons who had been killed after the fall of Srebrenica, the reburial operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one clarifying question, Mr. Nicholls. The Prosecution's estimate for time for the examination-in-chief was nine hours. Is this still the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to finish quite soon, Your Honours. To be honest, I'm not sure how much time I've used exactly, but I'll be wrapping up in -- I think I've got less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You, I think, used about six hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- roughly. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nicholson [sic], I'm not sure what the Chamber is interested in. There is a lot of things I can say about this, because I know exactly how the operation developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: Let's start in September 1995. Did you discuss this topic or receive orders on this topic from Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in September 1995 my brigade was visited by Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic from the Drina Corps command, including myself. He conveyed an order or information that the Main Staff ordered a -- that relocation be carried out of the mortal remains of the Muslims buried in the graves in Glogova. They were supposed to be taken out of the grave and placed in another location in the municipality of Srebrenica because Glogova was in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did that ordered relocation take place?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The order was carried out, and the operation naming my brigade was called "asanacija," sanitation and hygiene measures operation. It was implemented in keeping with the orders of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And which bodies took part or assisted in this, talking about VRS, MUP, civilian protection? Which of these different bodies took part?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this operation, starting with the idea of bodies being relocated and ending with the relocation itself, the following structures were involved: It included representatives of the political predominantly executive authorities in Bratunac; that is to say, the Executive Council and its president, the municipal president, and the chief of MUP. Then it included representatives of companies which had machinery such as ULTs, excavators, and other construction machinery that was needed for such an operation. In terms of construction companies, it included the Rad Bratunac public utility company. Then there was machinery from the state-owned company, the brickworks, in Bratunac. Next, from Srebrenica, there were also some companies taking part, such as the socially owned construction company Radnik and their machinery, and the Sase mine construction machinery as well as trucks. There were also trucks of the Autoprevoz company in Srebrenica. I may have forgotten some, but probably not. That's which companies took part. As for the military, the task was issued to the Bratunac Brigade because the graves were in its area of responsibility. The military police of the Bratunac Brigade take part. They secure the road between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac and Bratunac and Ljubovija. In addition to the military police, the civilian police took part as well, that is to say the public security station from Bratunac. They were engaged on the same tasks with the military police. They secured the roads together between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje and Bratunac and Ljubovija. They diverted all traffic to another road. As for the Drina Corps, there was the 5th Engineering Battalion with their machinery, and it is also important to note that the fuel for the operation was provided by the Drina Corps command on two occasions: The first time around 5 tonnes of oil and the next time about 2.5 tonnes of oil or fuel. All that was preceded by a number of meetings held at the Bratunac municipality premises in the office of the municipal president. He undertook upon himself to communicate with the companies so that the part of work not related to the military be carried out. They needed to provide machinery needed for the operation. It lasted from September on, for some two months, with several breaks due to a number of problems. In any case, the whole thing took about two months. Right at the outset, it was supposed to be secret, and I knew that as the chief of security. However, given the number of participants and the number of workers from the public utility company and the number of military and civilian policemen and other bodies, also given the number of assets that was required such as trucks, excavators, ULTs and other machinery from a number of construction companies, it was for all -- because of all that that the operation was no longer secret. That was the original intention. But, in my view, it cannot be deemed covert because everyone knew that the implement -- that the operation was implemented or carried out. That is it in briefest possible terms. If there's anything else you want to know, please ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just quickly show you a document, 65 ter 02084. Can we have the first page, please. Now, in the translation which will come up in a minute, I hope, it says, "Reports, meetings, 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade." Thank you. Just quickly, do you recognise this document, Mr. Nikolic? This book, rather.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. These are briefings from my 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this book, or who took the notes in this book or how was it used?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These briefings, or, rather, minutes from meetings of units from brigades including my own were written up for the sake of keeping records so that people could see what it was that was discussed at meetings, and it was basically the command of the brigade, the commander and his assistant commanders, and sometimes at such a briefing commanders of battalions would also be present and also of other units depending on what the meeting would focus on. So this is a document that is permanently kept in a brigade, and there are minutes kept at each and every meeting of this kind that is held.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please make sure to speak into the microphone. Otherwise, we cannot hear him well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, could you speak into the microphone for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to page 11 of the English, 24 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, here we have in the working meeting of commander with command staff and battalion commander from 16 October 1995. We see at the top Colonel Blagojevic speaking. Can we roll down to the bottom of each page, please. This is an 8.00 a.m. meeting that ended at 10.00 a.m. First of all, Mr. Nikolic, we see the name Nikolic written there in the notes of this meeting. Do you know if that's referring to you or if it's somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. These are minutes from a meeting in my brigade, so Nikolic, that is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we see the three points that are recorded that you said, and I'm looking at the third one today at the moment, which states in the English: "We are currently engaged in task issued by Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff (hygiene and sanitation measures)." Is that what it says in your version? I don't -- if you could read out the last point under your name.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are currently working on obligations given by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and then in parentheses, hygiene and sanitation measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the word in your language is "asanacija," is that right, that's written there, if I pronounced it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And what does this entry refer to? What are you saying -- what are these tasks? What's going on?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about what I read out just now, then at this meeting I reported to my commander saying that currently I was working on -- I mean, I meant the military police, because when the komandir is not there, then I usually do what they do. I usually say what it is that they were doing. So I informed my commander that I worked on the tasks that we had been given by the Main Staff, and they have to do with sanitation and hygiene measures. I already explained that the operation of relocation from Glogova was called "asanacija" in my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. So this entry, just to be clear, refers to that relocation operation in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This point that I read out just now refers to what you said, but the note refers to many other things, but specifically the point that we discussed just now has to do with the relocation from Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I tender perhaps the cover page and that page or whichever parts Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, two pages, the first page and the last page. That will be admitted as the next Prosecution exhibit, i.e., Exhibit P4391.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if it is acceptable to Your Honours, but I wonder if we might take the break now. I'm just about done, but I wouldn't mind taking a quick look to check over my materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for an hour and resume at 1.25. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.22 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, yesterday we discussed in the beginning that you had entered a guilty plea before this Tribunal and taken responsibility and accepted responsibility. I just want to ask you if you'd like to tell the Trial Chamber how you feel about what happened in Srebrenica and what happened to the Bosnian Muslim population in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever I testify, I take the opportunity to express my regret for everything that happened over there. I am absolutely aware of the fact that a terrible crime was committed in Srebrenica, that people were killed, that many families lost their children, their sons, their fathers, their brothers and sisters, and everything else. I personally feel responsible, and it's particular difficult for me because I worked in the school where many of those who lost their lives were provided with an education, and I quite simply wasn't able to help those who lost their lives, though I had -- I didn't have the courage to do that. Perhaps I helped certain individuals, my Muslim friends who were friends even before the war, but that wasn't sufficient, and yet again I'll use this opportunity to apologise to all the families and to all the victims of the crimes that were committed there. I want to say that I'm extremely sorry for having been there, for having carried out the orders I was given and for having contributed to the perpetration of the crimes committed in that way. I want to apologise to all the victims of the crime once more, and I'm very sorry that I did not flee when it became certain that these things were going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good day, Your Honours. Good day to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank you for being so kind as to meet with me and the Defence, and I believe that we agreed that we should try to determine the truth with as much precision as possible, whatever that truth might be, and I believe that you will assist us in attaining this objective. Thank you once more. Could we see P4391, a fairly fresh item, and I would like you to have a look at a detail in that document. E-court, P4391, and I would like to ask you whether you knew many of those people, Serbs and Muslims. I apologise. 4390, the previous one, 4390. Did you personally know many of those people? You said a minute ago that you taught some of them.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have in front of me -- well, now I have nothing in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4390. 02123 is the 65 ter number. That should be the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show the witness the written part, handwritten part. Probably page 3. Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we enlarge this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the part that concerns wounded Muslim out of 23 who remained after the evacuation which was organised by the ICRC, and he was handed over to the Zvornik CSB. This is dated the 18th of July; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Halilovic, Osman is the name of the enemy soldier. Did you know this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I knew quite a lot of Halilovics from Bratunac and Srebrenica. To be quite frank, I can't tell you whether I knew this particular Halilovic, but I can tell you that I knew a lot of people personally from the area of Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember how old this Halilovic was, the one referred to in this report?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's something I have to say for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, and this has to do with Halilovic. He is referred to in this report, but there is also a written report that concerns him alone that I provided to the Drina Corps command, and it's a man who is middle-aged or perhaps even younger. I don't want to speak off the top of my head, but I know exactly who is concerned, and I know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he arrested and handed over to the CSB in Zvornik in the area of responsibility of your brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't arrested. He was one of the wounded who were provided with accommodation in the health centre in Bratunac, and then the CSB officials took charge of him. He was on their list as someone who had committed a war crime. And operations officers from the State Security Service in Zvornik took charge of him and took him for further processing in the Zvornik centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened in the end? You don't know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I do. Osman Halilovic was interviewed. He was processed, and I don't know what the results of the process were, but according to the information I had, he was processed or he was taken before the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. We'll try and locate that case to see which Osman we are actually dealing with. Thank you very much. As you've already told us in the interview, you don't know much about police affairs, but very briefly, you held an important position from 1986, and that position had to do with the system of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: You don't know much about political events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to be precise for the sake of the Trial Chamber, in our interview I said that I was not someone who officially participated in political events because I wasn't part of the legislative or executive authorities, but naturally with regard to the political events, I, as someone who was involved in intelligence work, know many things about such political events, but I have told you that I'm not a credible witness when it comes to such matters because I wasn't a participant in the political life of the country, and I wasn't a member of a single political organisation -- or, rather, of the SDS which was in power at the time. And in response to your second question, yes, in 1986 I left the secondary school I was working in and started working in the Territorial Defence Staff, and I was assistant commander for intelligence in the Territorial Defence Staff in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the end of the interpretation, so please could you try to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try and take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What subject did you teach in secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for about five academic years, and during that period of time I taught defence and protection. That was the name of the subject that was a regular subject in secondary schools at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that subject have to do with the laws on All People's Defence and of the self-protection of a society, and did it have to do with Tito's doctrine as a whole on an armed people?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that subject, the subject of defence and protection, had its own curriculum, and it also included the field that you have just mentioned. I could agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then tomorrow we will ask you to clarify certain matters with regard to that subject, but something that we could have a look at now is the following: On page 59 the order "asanacija" was mentioned taking sanitation and hygiene measures or cleaning the terrain. Would you agree that "asanacija," taking such measures, is something that is covered by the law, and the civilian protection has to take such measures in peacetime and in wartime, in peacetime after catastrophes have occurred and in wartime after there has been a battle?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. I am a professor, and I dealt with that field. I know exactly what measures of sanitation and hygiene concern. It's a measure for civilian protection that is taken as a preventive measure. If that's not possible, hygiene and sanitation measures are taken in order to remove the results of catastrophes, natural catastrophes, or the results of war and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This includes removing the corpses or remains of animals or people. It also has to do with removing the results or eliminating the results of any kind of extraordinary activities or events.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the event, on the misfortune. So what taking hygiene and sanitation measures involves depends on the event itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a legal obligation, taking such measures is a legal measure that has to be taken. It is not a matter for someone to decide on voluntarily; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every social community takes sanitation and hygiene measures because it's in their own interest. I agree with you that this is a legal obligation and it is not a matter of someone's individual will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the period prior to the war, very briefly, you were in that position from 1986 up until the time when the war broke out, and during that period of time you had the opportunity, did you not, to report on or find out about reports on the possibility of threats to the security of the country or threats to the security of the armed forces; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your question were more precise, perhaps I could provide you with a more precise answer. But as a rule, given the position I occupied, I had the opportunity to obtain information of that nature as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say that the Territorial Defence at all territorial levels was an integral part of the armed forces of Yugoslavia and at the same time it was administratively considered to be part of the municipality's defence, and the president of the municipality, given his position, was the president of the council for defence and there was also a municipal brigade for the Territorial Defence, for territorial protection, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What you said contains some precise elements and some imprecise elements. I'll try and assist you. The armed forces of the former SFRJ were supposed of the JNA and the Territorial Defence. These were two parallel and equal components. So the TO - you asked me about the TO, the Territorial Defence - was one of the component parts of the armed forces of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. It was organised, on the whole, at the republican level. Every republic had its own Territorial Defence, and every municipality at its own level had municipal Territorial Defence. The highest level of organisation in the municipality in terms of command was the Territorial Defence Staff, the Municipal Staff, of course; and the highest level of organisation for the units on the territorial or municipal principle were the Territorial Defence detachments. So these were units the strength of a battalion. In brigades or in independent battalions they were a little more numerous than is the case for classical traditional battalions. Within the municipal Territorial Defence, in addition to these municipal staffs, there were sector staffs which were formed in local communes that covered a large territory and a detachment would be formed in that kind of a local commune which was extensive in territorial terms. In addition to detachments, there were Territorial Defence companies and there were independent platoons within the Territorial Defence system. So that was the structure of the Territorial Defence from the top to the municipal level, and it's true that the Territorial Defence was led by and supplied by the organs of the social and political community. The president of the municipality, in fact, was the president of the council, as you have said. But when it comes to command, the next level of command is the level of District Staffs and the district staff of Bratunac and Srebrenica was the Tuzla district staff. So that is the staff that was responsible for the training, the control, and the equipment of the Territorial Defence at the level of the municipalities of Bratunac and Srebrenica. And then there was the republican staff with the centre in Sarajevo, and this was the highest level of supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. It will be useful. Am I correct in saying that this entire structure that you have just described is a structure that also exists in peacetime not just in wartime, and it functions in peacetime and keeps one in a state of combat readiness for the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know it all, and I am going to explain this for the benefit of the Chamber. You know that the JNA and it's staffs, commands and units for the most part were units that were manned up to the maximum levels in principle. As opposed to the units of the JNA, staffs and commands and units of the TO were not a standing force. There was always a nucleus of such formation only and frequently they differed. For example, a peacetime TO staff greatly differed from a wartime TO staff. But in any case, your statement that there were staffs within the organisational schemes as well as commands and units that were manned, it meant that they could mobilise personnel. The weapons and equipment was provided as such at Municipal TO staff levels and in case of need there were draft calls and the manning was brought up to necessary levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will try to put simple questions that will hopefully be answered with a yes or no. You agree then that there were weapons in the municipalities and companies belonging to the TO and that the whole country was basically packed with arms. There were depots in municipalities, local communes, and companies?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the thrust of your question. The weapons of the units, staffs, and commands of the TO was in TO warehouses that were controlled. Some of that -- those weapons, since in addition to the units I mentioned there were companies which had their own TO units, which meant that those weapons held by companies, for example, the Vihor company had a company in my area the weapons were their property and was stored on their premises as well as the equipment they had. So there is a slight difference between what you said and what I have just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It means that they paid for it with their own money with the agreement of the TO, of course, and then they used the weapons to arm their own company. In other words, the weapons were their property.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a legal procedure which was to be followed which prescribed the way in which a company could procure military weapons and equipment, and there was -- there was also regulation in place as to its safekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that between the beginning of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the establishment of Republika Srpska and the VRS when it split from the JNA on the 19th and 20th of May, that the TO municipal brigades and staffs existed as a tactical reserve of the JNA and that they continued to exist within the VRS as regular units? Or to be more precise, who defended Bratunac before the VRS was established?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the brigades of the VRS were formed, all defence activities were under the competence of the units, commands, and staffs of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that not only in Bratunac but across the republic such brigades became municipal units, basically enjoying their logistical support and payment? In other words, they had very strong ties with their respective municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with that. The mechanism of manning such units even before the VRS brigades were formed and following that was based on the territorial principle. In other words, if you were to form a brigade in the area of Bratunac, it automatically meant that you manned your unit with the people from the municipal territory, and this functioned at all levels up to the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As an officer, do you see a difference between a people's army which is distributed territorially because it meant that people had their families there who were under the attack of another side's army which was again based on territorial principles, as opposed to a regular standing army where we have professional soldiers and their families are not involved in all that is happening?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very complex question, but I'll try to be brief. Concerning your question, I can say that there was a huge difference between TO units and professional JNA units which were present there. Now, as for any analysis of everything else you've mentioned, I'd rather not go there, but in any case, my answer is that, yes, there was a noticeable difference between the units manned by such soldiers as farmers, teachers, musicians who were there to man the TO as compared to professional units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I put this question because of what you said at page 20 yesterday where you said that there was some irresponsible people who used snipers to shoot around Srebrenica, contrary to what the orders were. This element, this fact that people knew each other and that they had personal motives such as revenge and because of the fact that their families were at stake, did it all multiply the possibility of such irresponsible incidents of people who did not wait for any orders to start shooting or even disobey it? I'm trying to gauge the contribution to this whole tragedy of the fact that these were not professional armed forces but, rather, simple people who were literally in the midst of a civil war.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'd rather not go into such speculations. To each and every one of your questions I could go into a deep analysis of what I think of the matter, but in this specific instance, in my understanding, what you are referring to cannot be included as an element in the whole situation. I don't think there is a causal relationship between the fact that someone was not a professional soldier but was still on a front line and fired upon a non-military target. My understanding of this whole thing is the following: It is completely irrelevant whether someone is a professional or not. If you wish to engage a non-military target, you may do so no matter how professional you are. So I see no direct link between what you are trying to establish, that is to say, between amateurism, so to speak, and illegal opening of fire from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I did not mean to involve amateurs. What I meant to say was that a professional soldier's family was far away from any theatre of war, whereas this people's soldier was in the middle of it, and you mentioned yourself in a number of cases that there was this danger of personal revenge, and you said that you had to secure the prisoners. I'm interested in the following: I am not referring to specify incidents, but was there this element of personal revenge which was increased multifold in this situation where we had two people's armies opposing one another as opposed to an international conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to take part in the professional force. I can only cite my experience from the people's army, as you call it, which existed at the level of municipalities. I can confirm that revenge was one of the causes of people being killed on both sides, but again I'll strive to be precise. I think that taking revenge only involved individual cases. And in this specific situation of Srebrenica and Bratunac, it did not play a role. There were individual instances of revenge and murders, and we are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Speaking of uncontrolled shooting, on page 20 yesterday, you also referred to that. I wanted to clarify this. Is it more difficult for an officer to control such an army when there are soldiers whose families' lives are at stake than it would be for an officer to command a professional army? As an officer, would you agree that it would be more difficult to control?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there is this military rule: The more professional your army is, the better trained it is, the less problems you have and the easier they are to control. And the other way around: If you have amateurs in your units, people who are unprofessional or poorly trained or who have been trained a long time ago, of course it is much more difficult to command and control such a force as opposed to a professional force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another brief question. During that period between 1986 and 1991 when Croatia and Slovenia seceded, through your intelligence channels did you receive information that perhaps a situation might occur in which a civil war was imminent or at least possible? Did you follow developments in your area and did the army and the TO -- well, in other words, you, as an intelligence officer were, busy doing something at the time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an intelligence organ in the pre-war period, I worked on similar things as during the war. I have already told you what it was I did during the war. However, there is another situation which is an imminent threat of war and the situation which makes it possible. The year when I joined the staff, or two, three, or four years later, it was the specific situation during -- because of which I kept receiving information such as the things you refer to. At the municipal level, that is to say my level, I also received information about a possible conflict, a possible war and inter-ethnic clashes in our municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the pre-war period, did you take note of the fact that the Drina division was established? I think that's the name it had. It was established by a former professional officer, Nurif Rizvanovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Nurif Rizvanovic personally, and I know what activities he engaged in. We did have information that Nurif Rizvanovic, who otherwise hails from Glogova, that during the time just before the war, was busy arming, raising funds, and bringing in weapons to the people in the area of villages around Glogova, including Hranca, Konjevic Polje, Sandici, et cetera. In that regard, I did have information about his activities, and I reported it to my superior at the district staff in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps slightly less importance, but nonetheless important for the Chamber to know, is it true that he was one of their leaders at the beginning of the war and that Oric and Tursunovic literally killed him off? There seems to have been some court-martial involved?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the 28th Division. I did not have such information, and I think his activities cannot be put in the context of the 28th Division activities during that time. Later on, yes, but not during the time you refer to. I know of an incident, and I do have information about what happened with Mr. Rizvanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that he was liquidated by Oric and Tursunovic, members of his own ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the information I was able to gather during the war and later point in that direction. It seems that during a visit by Oric and Tursunovic to Konjevic Polje where he was commander, they took him along on route to Tuzla but killed him along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As an intelligence officer, did you have insight into the formation of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, or, rather, what Sefer Halilovic was doing already from April 1991 onwards? And from that point of view, was Podrinje, the Drina River Valley very important for them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, I had information about the establishment of units and staffs by the Patriotic League. However, I never dealt with that level, if you will. I dealt with the activities that were at the level of my municipality. I knew -- actually, I knew things that were important in relation to the establishment and formation and arming of -- actually, that were a consequence of the orders that came from the leadership of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was my information correct, and we heard some of that here, namely that Muslims in Bratunac itself were not that militant? However, in Hranca, Glogova, and other Muslim concentrations they had units that were armed and that they had a parallel organisation of their own even before the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that in the territory of the municipality of Bratunac there are villages or local communes that were more militant than the centre of town itself. I can mention a few of them. For example, Glogova - you've mentioned it as well - a very militant area, a big local commune; and Konjevic Polje, likewise; and part of Voljavica and Zaluzje, extremely militant. Anyway, the town of Bratunac itself and the inhabitants of the town of Bratunac were less quarrelsome and less militant when compared to Glogova, Voljavica, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Osman Malagic from Voljavica, before he got killed in July or August, already gained fame as a military leader who led actions against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the Malagics from Voljavica, but believe me -- well, I had records of all excessive conduct and activities, but it's been 20 years now and I really cannot recall each and every instance, names and incidents pertaining to that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more political question: Did you notice that just before the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina the Serb side gave up on its struggle for Yugoslavia and that it was the reorganisation of Bosnia that was on the agenda, and from at that point of view there were political agreements that were conducive to the establishment of two municipalities in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I know all of this that you've mentioned. I also know about the initiative in Bratunac to establish the Serb municipality of Bratunac and the Muslim municipalities of Bratunac. And if you're interested, I even know the details in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that agreements were already underway and that peacefully and lovingly the transformation of the police into two police stations had already taken place in these two municipalities, or give us another detail of your own choice.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I heard here was peacefully and lovingly. No, there was no love. Peace, yes. There was no love whatsoever, and it wasn't naive at all. And it wasn't peaceful at all. I'll tell you what the truth is. The truth is that the quarrels broke out precisely because of these divisions. In a police station -- or, rather, in this single building, there was the police, public security station, and the Muslim public security station in the very same building. In the very same office you'd had a Serb duty officer and a Muslim duty officer. One would be the duty officer of the Muslim police station, and the other one of the Serb police station. And then there was this division of the territory of the municipality of Bratunac into the territory of the part of the municipality of Bratunac that was declared the Serb municipality of Bratunac, and the other one was the Muslim municipality of Bratunac. You know what it was like to divide Bratunac in that way? Practically that was impossible. It is not possible even in theory to make that kind of division. I'll just give you one example: You have Bratunac towards Kravica and Konjevic Polje, and then the next village is Vekocvac [phoen] which is Serb village. The next village Hranca is partly Muslim, and then the next part, about 20 per cent of that village is Serb, and then the next village is Glogova where there is a 100 per cent Muslim population, and then the next village is Kravica that is 100 per cent Serb, and so on and so forth. And now you're trying to divide something and then you also have these villages where the percentage is half/half, 60 per cent/40 per cent, and so on and so forth. Well, furthermore, what was very wrong was the fact that this division went on. Then they even divided companies. When they divided companies, then Serbs who worked in Muslim companies, I mean those that were given to the Muslims, then they started laying off Serbs, and they started replacing them by Muslims who then got jobs in these companies. This was chaos. After all of that, when all of this was created, this total confusion, then they established check-points. So say you set out to Konjevic Polje, you're stopped in Repovac after 2 kilometres first, and then after 3 kilometres you're stopped in Glogova, and then after 4 kilometres you're stopped in Kravica, and then in Sandici after yet another kilometre. So that was it. I am telling you practically what was happening on the ground and this happened in all directions. So there would be a Muslim village that had its own guards, its own roadblocks, its own check-points. Every Serb village would have its own check-point and roadblock. So you had a town that was absolutely divided. Bratunac is a very small town. So you have this political division, and it was exactly on an ethnic basis. All the Serbs were on the side of the SDS, all the Muslims were on the side of the SDA, and then there are police institutions that are divided, then the business sector is divided, and then there are these check-points, police check-points, and there is restricted movement, there. And within all of that you have activists that are being armed on both sides. The Serbs are arming their own, the Muslims are arming their own, and all of this is done illegally, under quotation marks. I follow this professionally and I knew exactly how these weapons were being brought in and how all of this happened and I reported on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: If you were chief of police or at the position that you did hold, as for Glogova, would you send ethnic Serb policemen or ethnic Muslim policemen to chase criminals there? Would it become complicated if you were to send a Serb team or a Serb patrol, a predominantly Serb patrol, say, to Glogova? Or if you would send Muslims to a Serb village at that time, in those times of distrust, would that have been a risk?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you take that context, the one that you are referring to and the time and all the divisions that were carried out, of course my answer is going to be negative, that I would never send Serb policemen to Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the other way round?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the other way round as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the first division occurred on the 31st of August, roughly, when the JNA was prevented from obtaining mobilisation documentation from the military department in Bratunac? Did about 10.000 SDA supporters assemble then, preventing the JNA from taking these documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know for sure is that members of the JNA -- or, rather, the team that came over to take these documents from the Secretariat for National Defence from Bratunac were prevented from doing this. This was the first organised conflict and protest in Bratunac that had been organised by the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct, do you agree, that there were quite a few armed actions already in March and that they were organised by Muslim paramilitaries, including sabotage and armed actions as such?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Karadzic, could you be more specific. Can you give us the year you mean? March which year? What is the year that you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. 1992. March 1992. That is to say, before the war break out. During the Lisbon negotiations, is it correct that already from the month of March onwards the Muslims were organising these actions? During the interview I handed some material over to you where they specify all the things that they did.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conflicts, armed conflicts, in the month of March 1992. As far as I know, there weren't any in the territory of Bratunac. Disagreements, quarrels, protests, yes, that kind of thing did happen. If you jog my memory, if you remind me of a specific action from that period, perhaps I may remember, or if you show me a document. However, as far as I know, there weren't any armed conflicts in the month of March in the territory of the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you are going to restrict yourself only to Bratunac, then I am not going to pursue the matter any further. However, can I count on the following, that after the war broke out, you knew quite a bit about Srebrenica as well, not only Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Srebrenica, once the war broke out, I knew quite a few things, and of course I will tell you about everything that I know, and if I don't know about something, I will tell you I don't know about that, so I'm not going to speak about anything that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 18th of April, 1992, as you said to us yesterday, you were mobilised and you became assistant commander for intelligence affairs. Let me ask you the following: Do you remember at the time you were in the Territorial Defence, do you remember that Mr. Izetbegovic declared general mobilisation on the 4th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I know that in April general mobilisation was declared. I don't know the date exactly. I do not remember -- actually, I didn't focus on that, but I do know that mobilisation was declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 8th of April the commander of the republican Territorial Defence, General Vukosavljevic, was dismissed, and on the 8th of April, Izetbegovic established a new Territorial Defence that did not include us, and he declared a state of imminent threat of war, and we did that on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these activities at the level of the republican staff or at the level of the Presidency, what Alija Izetbegovic did I cannot give you affirmative or precise answers there, but I was informed about the activities that had to do with the Territorial Defence, namely the disintegration of the existing Territorial Defence and the establishment of a new one. That I did know at the level of my municipality. I took part in the establishment of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You became assistant commander for intelligence, and I think that yesterday you said that for a while you also worked on security affairs as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Bratunac Brigade was established, that is to say in 1992, from its very establishment until the end, I was the chief for intelligence and security affairs in the Light Infantry Brigade in Bratunac, that is to say throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an assistant for intelligence and another assistant for security, or did you do all of it, because it wasn't a big brigade? Did you do it separately, or did you do all of it yourself?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the establishment of the Light Infantry Brigade, the organ for intelligence and security has a chief and also an officer for intelligence affairs. At one point I did have such an officer. From time to time I would have one, and then there were some periods when I did not have anyone else, when I was there on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did tell us, didn't you, that you reported to your brigade commander, according to the chain of command, and that professionally you had your chain to the same kind of service in the corps command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the same valid in the other direction as well, that is to say that down these chains from the corps command you would get orders or instructions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the sense of command, one receives orders from one's superior command. In terms of professional reporting, one receives instructions from one's superior instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To be more precise, if you received two contradictory orders from the brigade commander and from the corps command, from your intelligence and security superior instance, which of them would take precedence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's a hypothetical question which is exactly that, hypothetical. There is a rule. There is a law. Security or intelligence organs are managed and commanded by the commander of the unit that you are part of. Immediate command over security organs is in the hands of my brigade commander. He was authorised to manage, control, and command. In professional terms, there was also professional management which follows the other line, the intelligence and security line. At brigade level, there was no one who managed me professionally. The next higher level that was in charge of that was the chief of intel and security organ from the Drina Corps. That was the rule. There are exceptions, though, if you are in the field or in combat, as well as when the commander is absent, but there are officers there from a senior command, and each of those exceptions is then considered separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood properly, if there is a senior staff member visiting, he has primacy. He calls the shots if he's there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, no. I'll use a practical example. There is the Bratunac Brigade. If the corps commander is there and tells the brigade commander, As of today I'm here, and I will command and control the operation, then as was his right, he undertook upon himself to command in the AOR of my brigade. However, irrespective of his presence in the AOR, if he did not take over responsibility, it is the brigade commander who continues to command the brigade that he is in charge of. So there is no delegation of responsibility or command by virtue of your arrival in the area. That's the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me see if I understood that correctly. The security component is in a way more attached to the brigade, because the task is to secure the brigade, its soldiers and assets. You discussed that in the Blagojevic case in 2003 at page 1606. You said there that the duties involved were to plan and propose security measures with the aim of protecting the forces and assets as well as equipment and everything else that may be in danger in case of an enemy attack, or in case of any operation coming from outside of the unit. In that sense you are linked to the brigade and its security; correct? Your tasks also included any potential threats or acts of treason, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. When it comes to intelligence and security matters, I am, first and foremost, attached to the brigade, linked to the brigade. In all intel and security matters, as well as counter-intelligence, I am exclusively tied to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that regard, as was probably the case, you were supposed to know everything about your brigade and soldiers. It's about ability, dangers, and operations aimed against the brigade from the outside.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpret's correction: From outside.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look jointly at intelligence and security, the priority task was to know the dangers, something that threatens the units. It is one's primary duty as an intel officer to know who is in front of you, who is your enemy and what his force is. Once you know that, once you know about the enemy, his intentions, operations, and strength, when you have had assessed all that well, based on it all, you plan or propose to the commander what needs to be done to repel or deter enemy activity in order to protect one's own units, personnel, equipment, assets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At transcript page 24568, said yesterday that there was an additional obligation, in terms of counter-intelligence, was to gather evidence, documents, and information about the crimes committed in the area of responsibility which included all units. Did it include any crimes committed by our soldiers as well as enemy soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what the practice was in my brigade. Documenting crimes was a permanent task. It had no time limit. That is to say, from the beginning until the end of the war, as security organ I gathered intelligence information and documented instances of crime which took place in the area of responsibility in my brigade on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So irrespective of who committed them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did it also include any crimes which took place outside of combat, which had nothing to do with the hostilities in question in times of cease-fire if such crimes included military personnel?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My activities predominantly covered military personnel. When speaking of our unit, it included the soldiers and officers of my brigade. I did not have a single case file which involved members of civilian structures or those who were not in the ranks of the unit. In that sense, I know nothing. As for the officers and soldiers of my brigade, I basically knew everything that went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next you said that given the fact that you are not a lawyer, you had an assistant who was supposed to put it in a legal framework. You said so on the same page of the transcript, 24568. The person in question was Zlatan Celanovic, who was a lawyer. He was supposed to draft a criminal report and include all the material you gave him in a legal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be more precise in answering your question, because not everything you said is correct. Zlatan Celanovic was a desk officer of the morale, religious, and personal affairs. He is a lawyer by profession, but he had an office with the police. All matters related to criminal law was something that he was in charge of. It meant interviewing POWs, people who fled to the other side, collecting documents about crimes committed by members of the Bratunac Brigade, drafting criminal reports, and submitting all evidence and reports to the brigade commander for signature. I took part in all that by way of information I had. I forwarded all such information to Zlatan Celanovic so that he could use that to further corroborate any criminal reports he was going to submit. That was my part in assisting his work. He, in turn, was obliged that once such documents were signed by the commander to forward them to the competent military prosecutor and military courts for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said in line 8 that he had an office with the police, did you mean the military police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had an office in the MP building, that is to say the military police of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You discuss your role vis-a-vis the military police in the Blagojevic case on page 1606. In that regard, you had the ability to propose the use of the MP company - or was it a battalion? - in keeping with any brigade commander's orders. You were also in charge of communicating with the civilian police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you. It was neither a company or a battalion of the military police. It was an MP platoon that was part of the Bratunac Brigade. As regards my relationship with the military police, it mostly had to do with the professional management of the Military Police Platoon, professional management. As for command and control of the military police, that was in the hands of the commander. The brigade commander was the officer who directly commanded and controlled the military police that was within his brigade's establishment structure. In this case it was Commander Vidoje Blagojevic. He was the officer who commanded and controlled Mirko Jankovic, commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us not forget to mention something from 1992 as we are to move to another year. Were you in Bratunac when different groups terrorised the town and did many things against the wishes of the Bratunac people before the 28th of May and then later on in late 1992 and early 1993? Can you tell us something about that situation? If not, we'll just move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Bratunac in early 1992. When we had an interview together, I told you during what time I was not in Bratunac. I was also there in late 1992, early 1993, and onwards. All I know from that period is something I'm willing to share with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember April 1992? Do you remember some unrest? Do you remember the arrival of a group from Voljavica which demonstrated and fired weapons all around Bratunac in early April?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early April in Bratunac municipality, I don't know what specific incident you have in mind, but there were lots of cases of demonstrations, violence, shooting, although there were no killings. However, the situation of April 1992 was very serious, very tense, and it was only a question of moment when there would be an armed conflict or a clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that as of the 17th of April on, some volunteers appeared, most of whom refused to join the JNA, and they terrorised both Serbs and Muslims around town? Do you have any such information or knowledge? The period I have in mind is the six weeks between the 17th of April and the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know exactly that in this period of time that you refer to volunteers appeared in Bratunac. They called themselves different names, from the White Eagles to Arkan's men. I don't even know all of their names any more. At any rate, these were people who were not from the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is what I know about these groups. What I'm saying to you now is based on the information I received from the state security organ from Ljubovija. I talked to them, and I simply wanted to check to see who this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, just for the Trial Chamber, so for information or help, you turned to a neighbouring municipality in Serbia. Ljubovija's in Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I received information that they were from Serbia, it was easiest for me to check through their organs who these people actually were, and on the Drina Bridge where people were crossing from Bosnia to Serbia, they would take these people's documents and check each and every one of them individually, and then they informed me about who they were. On the basis of the information I received from them, most of the people who came there were criminals. They were multiple offenders who had spent several years in prison several times. There were also psychopaths among them, sick people, people like that. So these groups that were there did the worst things in the beginning. First they started with looting, then abusing Muslims, then when there were no Muslims left, that is to say when the Muslims left the territory of the municipality of Bratunac, then they started stopping Serb people, barging into their homes, attacking Serb girls, women, et cetera. So we had lots of problems with these people who arrived in the beginning of 1992, and they spent quite a while in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the municipal authorities did not have the strength to deal with them and that individuals and representatives of the authorities advised Muslims to stay away until these groups would get expelled? If you knew about that, tell us. If you didn't, then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I had this information. I personally asked for a unit to come from Serbia and expel these people, and indeed when there were problems. An officer came from Pancevo. I will remember the name. I'm a bit tired now, I will remember the man's name. This was an officer who came with a unit of the military police, and the police stayed at a motel in Ljubovija, and he came to see me at the staff in Bratunac. I explained all of this to him. Beforehand, since on the other side in Serbia, in Gucevo, there was the Drina operations group and it was commanded by Commander Milosevic, I asked Milosevic to send someone there to place these volunteers under their control and expel them. He came and a meeting was organised between the president of the Executive Board, I think the president of the municipality was there as well, then the chief of the Ministry of Defence was there, I was there, then this officer who had come from Belgrade, and there was a priest. When I asked for that, Rodoljub Djukanovic, the president of the Executive Board, and the priest declared that I was a traitor who wanted to expel their liberators. During this meeting, the priest organised a group of women and men who came to protest in front of the municipality building while we were in that meeting. And then of course the man said, Mr. Nikolic, you see how people feel. I don't want to go into this. He got his police escort, and he left, and then they were simply no longer there. So that's the story about the volunteers in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then this priest left the church later on as well; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left everything. He was one of the men who abused the church, humanitarian aid, everything that went through him, and also he took advantage of these unfortunate people who went by what he said. And now because of Rodoljub Djukanovic, these same people who were involved in this protest in front of the municipality building were later abused by these people who they did not want to see expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the beginning of 1993, was there a group of important instructors there that imposed a reign of terror in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1993, there was this group of instructors, and as for this group and their activities and everything they did, I wrote a report. I'm not sure whether I also sent it to the Main Staff of the command of the Drina Corps. I'm not sure about that, but there is this report of mine from 1993 about their activities and everything that they did in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After a while you got rid of them, too, in a way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After lots and lots of problems that we had there, I personally had all these problems with them as well, but we did have very many problems that had to do with abusing people, beating up officers, beating up the brigade commander, kicking the brigade commander. And also we had this group of criminals that had come there. Quite simply, their basic objective was to take over power totally. There is a report to that effect. They did not dare attack the command of the brigade because I threatened that if they tried to do that as they did to the police, I threatened that I would come with the unit and with our combat resources and that I would destroy them. So they left me alone, and they left the brigade alone, but in this report it says that they looted, abused people, detained people. They beat the president of the municipality. They beat the president of the SDS. Your Miroslav Deronjic, they physically beat him, abused him. It was chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Jokic was a man's name, or whatever from Srebrenica, is also a high official from the SDS. They led him with his hands tied through town. Was this the first group or the second group?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the second group from 1993. And it's not only Jokic that they had tied up, also Delivoje Sorak, who was commander of the Territorial Defence Staff of Srebrenica at the time. They took him through town. They put a board around his neck in front of him and it says, Sorak Delivoje admits that he killed Goran Zekic -- or, rather, Delivoje and Goran Zekic were in the same car when Goran Zekic was assassinated, and then they put this board around Zorko's [as interpreted] neck and they took him out and paraded him through town for days and people spat at him because on that board it said, I killed Goran Zekic, but actually Delivoje is an honest man and he had nothing whatsoever to do with the killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Zekic, who was an MP and a judge, and he was killed on the 8th of May, and isn't it correct that he was killed by the Muslims after all, not Serbs? There's no dilemma about that; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no dilemma in this regard. On the basis of all the reports, all the interviews, all the evidence gathered, I'm sure, I'm convinced that he was killed by the Muslims and that Delivoje Sorak had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Excellencies, tell us, what is your next move? Are we going to call it a day or do we have more time left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn for today and resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of February, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.01 p.m.,
